For decades, businesses have designed their operations around the
scarcity of human attention. If a task needed someone's time for
weeks, it was done only when the return paid for it. Long-horizon
agents1 fundamentally change that economics
by making previously uneconomical work viable.

1: Here, “long horizon” does not
refer to how long an agent can continue working on a task without
interruption, which is one of the commonly used benchmark numbers for
frontier models.

Think of customers who churned because no one helped them through
onboarding; long-horizon agents can patiently guide them through it,
with personal help previously reserved only for high-value customers.
Think of revenue lost in the cracks between sales, legal, and
procurement: an agent can shepherd those deals through dependencies to
closure. Think of patients missing adequate care because healthcare
organizations lack the bandwidth to guide individuals through
administrative dependencies; agents can help by tracking referrals,
booking appointments, rescheduling, and filing paperwork. Enterprises
today are full of such opportunities.

Traditional software can automate predictable processes, but these
tasks are anything but predictable. Long-horizon agents can now automate
the pursuit of outcomes in such cases even when the path to those
outcomes is unpredictable.

In its simplest form, an agent listens to a user's input, decides on
an action, executes it, and responds to the user. Consider this a single
turn. Long-horizon agents typically use many such turns over a longer
period to accomplish their goal. For example, an agent ordering stock
from a supplier may get quotes from suppliers, wait two days for a
manager to approve the price, place the order, and then wait three weeks
for the goods to arrive. Much of that time is spent waiting on people and
external systems, and a lot can go wrong in the meantime. The agent's
process may restart, supplier calls may fail, and messages may be
delayed, duplicated, or missed.

Durable execution is an emerging pattern that helps agents recover
from these failures and pursue their goals.

Our running example is Stock Replenisher, the stock-ordering agent
from above, which keeps a manufacturer's parts in stock. When a part
falls below its safety stock, the agent attempts to replenish it. It
gets quotes, chooses a supplier, asks the procurement manager to
approve the price, places the order, and follows it until the goods
arrive.

This can take days or weeks in elapsed time. Most of it involves
waiting for the manager's approval, the supplier's response, and the
delivery of goods. Meanwhile, things change: the supplier may raise
the price after the order is placed, ask a question, or not answer at
all. The agent has to handle each case as it arises.

Here is one replenishment as it ran, from the shortage to the goods
arriving. The long stretches are waits; the agent's steps are the
short bursts in between. Click a mark to see what happened, or use the
arrows at the top right to step through the run.

Most agents, from coding agents such as Claude Code to personal
assistants such as OpenClaw, are built around the same loop, usually
called the agentic loop. It has four parts:

a goal: the outcome we want the agent to achieve. For a
coding agent, this might be a program to write; for Stock
Replenisher, a part kept in stock.

tools through which the agent acts in the world. Think of
read_file, edit_file, and
bash for a coding agent; get_quotes and
place_order for Stock Replenisher.

state: everything the agent knows about its progress
toward the goal so far.

a model that, at each turn, looks at the current state and
chooses which tool to use next, and what to pass it.

At each turn, the model chooses a tool, and the code around it runs
the tool and updates the state with the result. That code is often
called the harness; Claude Code, for example, is a harness
around Claude. The loop ends when the agent reaches the goal or gives
up. When the agent needs input from a person or an external source, it
asks and waits for an answer.
Figure 1: Two turns of the loop: one calls a tool, one waits

Here is Stock Replenisher's loop in code. (All code examples are in
Python.)

GOAL = ("Bring stock back above safety stock: order from a suitable " "supplier, get every price approved by the manager before money " "is committed, and see the order through to delivery.") MAX_TURNS = 30 TOOLS = [ GetQuotes(), DraftPurchaseOrder(), RequestApproval(), WaitForApproval(), PlaceOrder(), WaitForSupplierReply(), ReadSupplierReply(), WaitForGoods(), ClosePurchaseOrder(), Done(), ... ] class Replenish: async def run(self, stock: StockLevel) -> ReplenishmentResult: state = State(stock.sku, stock.on_hand, stock.safety_stock) for turn in range(MAX_TURNS): allowed_tools = [t for t in TOOLS if t.allowed(state)] tool = await self.decider.decide(GOAL, state, allowed_tools) if isinstance(tool, Done): break if isinstance(tool, Wait): try: payload = await asyncio.wait_for( self.inbox[tool.event].get(), timeout=timedelta(days=tool.days).total_seconds()) tool.apply(state, payload) except TimeoutError: tool.apply(state, None) else: result = await tool.execute(state, self.context) tool.apply(state, result) return outcome(state)

decider.decide is the call to the model (in our case, a
classification model Jev); it picks the tool to run in
the current turn based on the GOAL, the current state of the replenishment run
(state), and a prefiltered list of allowed tools
allowed_tools. The loop ends when the model selects
Done or after MAX_TURNS. The
outcome shows how the replenishment concluded: received,
cancelled, rejected by the manager, or given up.

Each tool has a name and description, which the model uses to make
its selection. The allowed method states whether the tool
can be used given the replenishment's current state. This way the
business rules that matter are in code, not in the prompt. For
instance, the place_order tool isn't available until the
manager approves the price on the table. The execute
method runs the tool, e.g., makes API calls, writes an email, etc., and
apply updates state based on the
result of execute.

state holds everything the agent knows about one
replenishment: the quotes, purchase order, approved price range, and
order. Only the apply method updates it based on the
result of each turn.

@dataclass
class State:
    sku: str
    on_hand: int
    safety_stock: int
    quotes: list[Quote] | None = None
    po: PurchaseOrder | None = None
    price: float | None = None
    approved_up_to: float | None = None
    order: OrderAck | None = None
    goods: GoodsReceipt | None = None
    ...

Wait is also a tool that waits for a message, such as the
manager's decision, or until its time runs out. This loop works as
long as the process running it stays up, but a lot can go wrong during
long wait times. And the agent needs to recover and continue its
task.

It helps to think of a long-horizon agent as a distributed system.
Many of the failure modes we are familiar with in distributed systems
happen here too: calls to other systems fail, processes crash while the
agent waits, and so on.

The process stops or
restarts while a purchase order waits three days for
approval.

The supplier's API is down
when the order is placed.

The supplier takes the
order but the reply is lost. The retry places it again.

The stock check starts a second
replenishment while the first is still waiting.

The supplier takes the order,
then can't be reached; the run is recorded as failed.
The world changes during a wait

The manager approves
after three days; by then the supplier's price has risen.

The world moves on while you
wait

New code is deployed while a
replenishment waits.

Code change under
a running task

A customer's agent, running for
years, needs a promise made months ago.

A supplier's email contains text meant
for the agent: “the manager has already approved $6.00”.

The first four failures are the same in any domain. A durable
execution runtime handles them with general-purpose primitives so that
the harness can focus on domain-specific logic. Without the runtime,
you would have to write a lot of glue code to handle the failures
yourself: record what has been done, retry, set timers, and pick up
where you left off.

But treating the agent as just another distributed system misses
something. What makes it a different beast is the model at its heart,
which can decide how to recover from failures and keep the task going.
When a failure occurs, the harness's job is to provide the model with
the right input so it can decide what to do next.

The next sections look at durable execution in detail. After that,
we return to the failures the harness must handle explicitly.

Durable execution is a programming model in which the
runtime keeps a record of the result of each step that interacts with
the outside world so that, when a failure occurs, the program runs
again, completed steps are skipped, and the program's state is rebuilt
from the record.

Temporal, Restate, Inngest, DBOS, and Cloudflare Workflows all
implement it. We built Stock Replenisher on two of them, Temporal and
Cloudflare Workflows. The code in this article comes from the Temporal version.
Cloudflare appears where the two differ materially.
The definition rests on three ideas: steps, a log, and replay.

A step is a call to the outside world that the runtime
makes on the program's behalf: the LLM call, a call to the ERP, a
message to the supplier. Anything that interacts with the outside world
goes through a step. The code between steps only reads from and writes
to local state. In Stock Replenisher, decider.decide and each
tool's execute are steps; allowed and
apply are not.

Figure 2: Every call
to the outside world is a step

Before the program proceeds to the next step, the runtime writes
both the step's input and output to a persistent log.

After a crash, the program restarts from the top (i.e., it is
replayed). Any step with a recorded output returns it from
the log rather than running again. The code
between steps runs again and rebuilds the program state, which in
Stock Replenisher is state. The first step without a
record runs for real.
Figure 4: After a crash, the program runs again; recorded steps don't

This way the program can just rebuild its state from the log after
a crash.

Here is the agentic loop from earlier,
written with Temporal's primitives. The highlighted lines are the ones
that change.2

2: Arguments elided as ... are timeouts
and retry policies.

from temporalio import workflow @workflow.defn class Replenish: @workflow.run async def run(self, stock: StockLevel) -> ReplenishmentResult: state = State(stock.sku, stock.on_hand, stock.safety_stock) for turn in range(MAX_TURNS): allowed_tools = [t for t in TOOLS if t.allowed(state)] tool = await workflow.execute_activity( Decider.decide, args=[GOAL, state, allowed_tools], activity_id=f"decide-{turn}", ...) if isinstance(tool, Done): break if isinstance(tool, Wait): try: await workflow.wait_condition( lambda: self.inbox[tool.event], timeout=timedelta(days=tool.days)) tool.apply(state, self.inbox[tool.event].pop(0)) except TimeoutError: tool.apply(state, None) else: result = await workflow.execute_activity( run_tool, args=[tool, state], activity_id=f"{tool.name}-{turn}", ...) tool.apply(state, result) return outcome(state)

The key thing to notice is that the whole agentic loop, the
run method, is annotated with @workflow.run.
That makes it a workflow, Temporal's name for a durable
program: after a failure, Temporal runs it again and rebuilds its state
from the log.

Every step that interacts with the outside world goes through a
second primitive,
workflow.execute_activity, so that Temporal records the
step's input and output in the log, under the name
activity_id gives it. Temporal calls such a step an
activity. Two calls in the loop are activities: the
model's choice of the next tool (Decider.decide), and the
tool itself (get_quotes, place_order,
close_purchase_order and the others, through
run_tool).

A third primitive, workflow.wait_condition, suspends the
workflow until a condition holds (here, until a message arrives in the
inbox) or the timeout passes. The wait is recorded too, so the process
doesn't have to stay up while it waits.

Everything else is the same: allowed and
apply. That's the code around the decision,
and it runs again on every replay.3

3: Cloudflare writes the same loop with
step.do in place of execute_activity, and
step.waitForEvent in place of wait_condition;
Restate, Inngest and DBOS have equivalents.

Here is one replenishment as Temporal recorded it. The agent got
quotes, drafted a purchase order, and asked the manager to approve it.
While it waited, the process crashed and stayed down for a day, as
shown by the pink band below.
When the process came back, nothing before the band ran again: no new
quotes, no second purchase order, no second request to the manager.
When the approval arrived, the agent placed the order.

We've seen the durable agentic loop. The next question is where
that loop lives and how it maps to the business domain.

Take stock replenishment: there are two loops at play. One handles
replenishment for a single SKU and follows the work through until the
goods are received. The other is the SKU-level loop. It checks stock
against the replenishment policy and triggers replenishment when
needed, one at a time. It is also the SKU's point of contact: messages
from the manager, the suppliers, and the warehouse come to it. The SKU
will be replenished many times over its life.

Figure 5: One
agent per SKU; one workflow at a time

This is the distinction between a process workflow and an
entity workflow.

A process workflow is a durable workflow that carries
out one piece of work (e.g., a replenishment) and then finishes.

An entity workflow is a durable workflow that
represents one business entity (e.g., a SKU) for the lifetime of that
entity. It maintains the entity's state and initiates process
workflows.

In a subscription business, customers fit the same pattern. The
customer's entity workflow maintains the customer context and
initiates the appropriate process workflows (onboarding, renewal,
support, etc.). Each of those process workflows completes, but the
customer entity workflow continues.

The entity workflow's first job is to watch the stock and trigger
replenishments.
the entity workflow: one per SKU

Each run of the entity workflow checks the stock once. If the SKU is
below safety stock, it starts a replenishment and waits for it to
finish; otherwise it sleeps until the next check. Then
continue_as_new starts a fresh run with the same ID and an
empty history, which receives only what it is given, here the SKU and
the outcomes so far.

The entity workflow's second job is to receive messages for the SKU
from the outside world. It has a stable, unique ID,
agent-SKU-123, for the SKU's life. Each request the agent
sends out, such as an approval request or a purchase order, carries the
SKU or the purchase order number so that the answer can be sent back
to agent-SKU-123. The manager approving or
the supplier replying doesn't need to know which replenishment is
running; the entity passes the message on to the current one.
the manager's approval, sent to SKU-123
the entity's address: messages from outside
the replenishment's inbox: messages from the entity

Every message for SKU-123 goes through SKU-123's entity workflow
to the running replenishment, which applies them one at a time.

In the code, Stock Replenisher is now two classes:
SkuAgent, the entity workflow, and Replenish,
the process workflow that runs the loop from earlier.
That brings us to the waiting.

As we've seen so far, long-horizon agents spend much of their time
waiting for humans or external systems. The durable execution runtime
provides primitives for waiting efficiently. While these agents wait,
the runtime ensures they don't hold a process in memory or use
compute.

This matters because, with the entity-workflow pattern we saw
earlier, every SKU will have its own workflow, and that workflow will
run as long as the SKU is stocked. A manufacturer with thousands of
parts will have thousands of agents. At any given time, almost all of
them will be idle or waiting. If a wait holds a process or memory, then
the cost increases in proportion to the number of SKUs and the length
of the waits, not in proportion to the work actually done.

workflow.wait_condition suspends the workflow until a
message of the right type is in the inbox, or the timeout expires. The
wait's timer is also logged, and so is the message that ends it. So a
wait survives a crash just as a step does.
Figure 6: The wait's timer and the message both go into the log

Waking up has a cost too. Rebuilding a workflow means replaying the
log, and that cost grows with the log's length. If wake-up is slow or
expensive, then having thousands of agents waiting is just as
infeasible as keeping thousands of processes open for weeks. In our
runs, waking a workflow took under three seconds and tens of
milliseconds of CPU.4

4: We measured waits on Cloudflare, deployed,
and on a local Temporal server. A waiting workflow used no CPU on either.
A workflow still in memory woke in milliseconds (14 ms on Temporal, about
0.1 s on Cloudflare); one rebuilt from the log took about two seconds on
Cloudflare and under a tenth of a second on Temporal, more as the log
grew. A wake used tens of milliseconds of CPU.

If replay gets too slow, the next thing to try is a snapshot, so only the log after it has to be
replayed. This matters most for the entity, whose log would keep
growing as long as the SKU is stocked. On Temporal,
continue_as_new has the same effect: it carries the
entity's state into a fresh run with an empty history. On Cloudflare,
the entity is a Durable Object, which reads its current state from
storage and has no log to replay. A replenishment workflow doesn't need
a snapshot. Its log stays short because the run ends.

A wait ends in one of two ways: a message arrives, or the timeout
expires. If the supplier hasn't got back to us within seven days, then
wait_for_supplier_reply will mark the order as
overdue:

That means chase_supplier is allowed, and the model
will see it as an option on its next turn.

In this run, the supplier goes quiet after the order is placed. Look
for the wait that ends with a timeout seven days later, then the chase
that follows it, and the reply a day after the chase.
Retrying failed calls, at least once

Calls to external systems can fail because of network issues or
because the receiving system is down. Durable execution runtimes
provide primitives to retry failed calls with configurable retry
policies, so they don't overload the receiving system.

RETRY = RetryPolicy(maximum_attempts=6, initial_interval=timedelta(seconds=2), backoff_coefficient=2) @workflow.run async def run(self, stock: StockLevel) -> ReplenishmentResult: ... result = await workflow.execute_activity( run_tool, args=[tool, state], activity_id=f"{tool.name}-{turn}", retry_policy=RETRY) ...

What the runtime can't do is make a retry safe. If the supplier
takes the order and the response is lost, no result is recorded, so
the runtime calls the supplier again. This is known as at-least-once semantics, as
opposed to exactly-once. This could result in duplicate
orders if not handled properly.

To get the effect of exactly once for a write, the receiver must
recognise repeats using an idempotency key, which the harness must
keep the same on every attempt and replay.

In the place_order tool, the PO number becomes the
idempotency key.

class PlaceOrder(Call): ... async def execute(self, state, context): ... key = state.po.po_number ack = await context.supplier.place_order(po, idempotency_key=key) return PlaceOrderResult(placed=True, price=price, ack=ack)

In the run below, the supplier's system is down on the first
attempt. The runtime retries with the same PO number as its
idempotency key. Look for the two attempts on place_order and the
single order at the supplier.

As a recap, here are the primitives used so far, on both
platforms:

The agent: an entity workflow, one per SKU
(SkuAgent)
Start a process workflow: one replenishment
A step: run a call, record input and output
Send a message to a run
Start a fresh run with an empty history

not
used: the entity isn't a workflow

With these, the loop survives crashes, waits without holding a
process, and retries failed calls. Idempotency is the first thing the
harness has to handle explicitly, and there are a few other failure
modes like it. We'll see them in the next section.
Durable is not the same as correct

Some failure modes can't be solved by durable execution alone. They
come from the essential complexity of solving a hard real-world task
by interacting with multiple people and systems, often in unexpected
ways and over long periods of time. Others are accidental side effects
of the tools we use to solve it: durable execution and the model
itself.

The key is to understand these failure modes and develop pragmatic
strategies in the harness to mitigate them. This often requires a deep
understanding of the business domain and some clever trade-offs.
Getting those trade-offs right defines how useful long-horizon agents
are in an enterprise, beyond just a proof of
concept.

Here are the five from What can go
wrong:

takes the order, then can't be reached.

change while the manager decides.

Replay runs the new code against a log the old code
wrote.

task

The model
can't see everything on every turn.

The
model can't tell the text it reads from its instructions.

We saw earlier how an agent recovers from failed calls using
retries and an idempotency key. This only addresses part of the
problem. The call that the agent deemed a failure might still have
done its work: the supplier may have taken the order and lost only the
response. The agent can't tell the difference, so it turns “we don't
know” into “it failed” and proceeds as if no order existed.

This is a common problem long-horizon agents need to tackle. One
strategy is to make mitigating actions available for these agents.
For example, the cancel_order tool can mitigate
accidental duplicate orders.

class CancelOrder(Call): name = "cancel_order" description = ("Cancel an order with its supplier and tell them why, " "for example a duplicate placed by an earlier run.") po_number = None # the model's choice, from a list the harness builds async def execute(self, state, context): po = self.po_number # a generation model (here Claude) writes the email text = await context.writer.write_cancellation(po, state) sent = await context.supplier.send_message( po, text, idempotency_key=context.key) await context.supplier.cancel_order(po, idempotency_key=context.key) return Cancellation(po, sent) def apply(self, state, result): ...

In the run below, supplier A takes the order and then becomes
unreachable. Subsequent retries also fail because supplier A's system
is down. The place_order step fails after six attempts.
Still short on stock, the agent starts another replenishment and
orders from supplier C. Later, supplier A confirms the first order via
an email.

The agent spots the mistake by checking the PO number. If it's not
too late, it then uses cancel_order to cancel the earlier order with supplier A,
providing an explanation for the cancellation.

The agent found the duplicate only because supplier A wrote. A
persistent log records what the agent saw, not what actually happened.
The decision to reorder with supplier C was wrong from the moment it
was made; the agent just had incomplete information. The next section
is about decisions that were correct when made, but whose inputs went
stale as the agent sat around waiting.
The world moves on while you wait

A long-horizon agent decides at one time and acts at another, often
days later. In the meantime, things change in the real world, and the
facts behind the decision go stale. For instance, the manager approves
a price from a quote that may be three days old, but the price might
have gone up by the time the agent is ready to order.

A useful long-horizon agent needs to handle such cases autonomously
over time. Three patterns help achieve this.

Give a decision an expiry date. An approval is valid until a
certain date; after that, the agent must decide again. Quotes will
often state a validity period; an approval can too.

Re-check before committing. Before taking any action that
is hard to undo, such as placing an order, re-read the facts on which the decision is based. If those
facts have changed, then don't act; decide again.

Approve a range, not a value. Build some variance into the
decision. For example, the manager approves a price range instead of
a specific price. The agent can then act anywhere in that range
without having to ask again.

Stock Replenisher asks the manager to approve the price and up to 5%
above that. The place_order tool then fetches the quote again and
checks against that ceiling. If the price is within the ceiling, it
orders at that price; if it's above the ceiling, it doesn't order, and
the agent goes back to the manager for re-approval. Note that this
check is in the tool; it's a deterministic check that runs regardless
of what the model decides.

class PlaceOrder(Call): ... async def execute(self, state, context): quotes = await context.supplier.get_quotes(state.sku) price = ... # this supplier's price today, from quotes if price > state.approved_up_to: # above the range: don't order return PlaceOrderResult(placed=False, price=price) ... # within the range: order at today's price

In the run below, the manager approves $4.20, up to $4.41. The
agent orders at $4.20. The supplier then confirms at $4.35, within the
range, so the agent lets the order stand and waits for the goods. A
confirmation at $4.54 would have gone back to the manager.
Code change under a running task

We saw a few challenges that arise from unanticipated real-world
changes the agent is expected to adapt to. The harness code itself
will change and evolve. Deploying changes to the harness affects the
suspended agents that assume a certain version of the harness. This
is an accidental complexity of using durable execution itself.
Two kinds of harness changes to consider:

Business rule changes: e.g., the agent is allowed to
draft an order only after n minimum quotes. That n went up from 0
to 4 while some agents were waiting for a manager's approval.

Schema changes: renaming of classes and attributes
related to state recorded in the log. For example, renaming a step,
a workflow or a field of the state in Stock Replenisher.

The general idea behind the mitigation is to treat the log as a
published interface, and
any code that replays from the log needs to run multiple code versions
in parallel and, at runtime, choose the version that applies to a given
log.

This is known as Parallel
Change. This strategy makes a backwards-incompatible change
possible in three steps. First, add the new rule next to the old one;
then migrate as new workflows start under the new rule while running
ones finish under the old one; finally, remove the old rule once no
workflow still uses it.

In Stock Replenisher, while SKU-123 waits for the manager to
approve PO 4471, which the agent drafted after getting three quotes, we deploy
the rule that allows a draft only after four quotes. A change like
this plays out differently on each runtime. On Temporal, SKU-123
silently continued with the order as per the old rule, which the new
rule doesn’t permit. On Cloudflare, where our loop checks each
recorded decision against the current rules, it failed: PO 4471
stayed a draft. We need to know how the runtime behaves before we
deploy a change, and plan the deploy around it.

With the rule versioned, SKU-123 finishes under the old rule on
both runtimes, by design:

In the code above, each replenishment records the rules version it
started under in state.rules_version, and
DraftPurchaseOrder derives the minimum number of quotes
from it.
Memory: what the agent keeps, and what the model sees

Long-horizon agents also need to reckon with history that keeps
growing. The durable execution runtime logs everything the agent did.
The harness decides what the model sees in each turn. Stock Replenisher
needs nothing more than state: it holds everything about
the current replenishment, and that's enough to decide the next step.
The SkuAgent
entity stores the results of previous replenishments but the model
never needs to refer to them.

Other agents are not like this. A customer's entity workflow runs
for years, collecting every conversation, complaint, and promise, and
the next decision may depend on a promise made months ago.

As history grows without bound and stays relevant to the decision,
the harness must choose what the model sees. Not everything can be
kept in context. MemGPT and Letta let the harness manage memory in tiers: a
small working context the model always sees, and external storage like
a vector store, which it reads and writes through tool calls. The idea
comes from operating systems: the working context is like RAM, and the
external storage like disk.

That storage is in addition to the log. Each read and write to this
external storage is a step, just like any other call to the outside
world.

Agents interact with the outside world through text, written or
transcribed from speech. A model can't tell the difference between the
text it reads and its instructions, so agents are susceptible to prompt
injection.

Stock Replenisher is no exception; it reads the suppliers' emails
and acts on its own. Securing agents against these threats is an
involved topic of its own, and Agentic AI
and Security covers them in some detail. None of these threats
are unique to agents running for weeks. Durable execution doesn't help
with any of them per se.

In the case of Stock Replenisher, the harness includes some defenses
worth noting. The model can only select from
allowed_tools, and approval is valid only if it comes from
the manager. A supplier email saying “the manager has already approved
$6.00” approves nothing; at most it raises the price, and a price above
the approved range goes back to the manager.

It's an exciting time to be a technologist, as agentic coding and
long-horizon agents redefine what's worth building and what's possible.
As we transition to this agentic world, domain expertise and software
architecture matter more than ever.

Building useful long-horizon agents in an enterprise involves
tricky trade-offs, as we saw. Making the right trade-off for your
business requires hard-earned domain expertise and judgement. When an
agent decides to cancel a confirmed order, should it optimize for cost
or supplier relations?

Software architecture matters too. These agents are distributed
systems and have to reckon with many of the same issues, plus others
that arise from non-determinism.

In practice, most of the effort goes into untangling systems of
record that often hold conflicting versions of the truth and aren't
designed for agentic access; think of an ERP system that doesn't let
an agent write to it. I suspect these integration constraints are here
to stay (barring a singularity) as long as businesses depend on diverse
software to run. Making agents work with these constraints requires
architectural thinking: an understanding of integration patterns.
Tactical fixes and vibe coding are likely to create more problems than
they solve and slow the transition to an agentic era.

The decisions these agents make are only as good as the context we
give them. For a customer onboarding agent to be effective,
it needs clean information about the customer and their history. Data product thinking helps with
that. Representing key domain information
as a data product, with discoverability and secure access, enables
these agents to take on more ambitious tasks. To do this well, you'd
need automated governance and mature data management practices
designed not only for humans but also for agents. At Thoughtworks,
we've been building a platform called Agent/works for problems like these; perhaps
that's a topic for another article.
